subject.name: Biology
subject.description: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (Extended). Sample content covers every syllabus topic. The questions are original practice questions written in the style of Cambridge papers, not reproduced past paper material.

topics.title: Characteristics and classification of living organisms
topics.summary: Characteristics of living organisms, the concept and uses of classification systems, features of organisms, dichotomous keys.

topics.title: Organisation of the organism
topics.summary: Cell structure, specialised cells, tissues and organs, size of specimens and magnification.

topics.title: Movement into and out of cells
topics.summary: Diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

topics.title: Biological molecules
topics.summary: Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, food tests and the structure of DNA.

topics.title: Enzymes
topics.summary: Enzyme action, specificity, and the effects of temperature and pH.

topics.title: Plant nutrition
topics.summary: Photosynthesis, leaf structure and mineral requirements.

topics.title: Human nutrition
topics.summary: Diet, digestive system, physical and chemical digestion, absorption.

topics.title: Transport in plants
topics.summary: Xylem and phloem, water uptake, transpiration and translocation.

topics.title: Transport in animals
topics.summary: Circulatory systems, the heart, blood vessels and blood.

topics.title: Diseases and immunity
topics.summary: Pathogens, transmission, defences and the immune response.

topics.title: Gas exchange in humans
topics.summary: Gas exchange surfaces, breathing and the effect of exercise.

topics.title: Respiration
topics.summary: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

topics.title: Excretion in humans
topics.summary: Excretory products, the kidney and the liver.

topics.title: Coordination and response
topics.summary: The nervous system, sense organs, hormones, homeostasis and tropic responses.

topics.title: Drugs
topics.summary: Medicinal drugs and antibiotics.

topics.title: Reproduction
topics.summary: Asexual and sexual reproduction in plants and humans, sex hormones, sexually transmitted infections.

topics.title: Inheritance
topics.summary: Chromosomes, genes and proteins, mitosis, meiosis and monohybrid inheritance.

topics.title: Variation and selection
topics.summary: Variation, adaptive features, natural and artificial selection.

topics.title: Organisms and their environment
topics.summary: Energy flow, food chains and webs, nutrient cycles and populations.

topics.title: Human influences on ecosystems
topics.summary: Food supply, habitat destruction, pollution and conservation.

topics.title: Biotechnology and genetic engineering
topics.summary: Biotechnology and genetic modification.

parts.prompt: Which characteristic of living organisms is described as 'the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism'?
parts.examinerComment: Candidates confused respiration with nutrition. Nutrition is taking in materials for energy, growth and development; respiration releases the energy.

parts.prompt: In the binomial system, which part of the name Panthera leo indicates the genus?

markingPoints.text: A – the first word is the genus

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: An organism has a body divided into three parts, three pairs of jointed legs and one pair of antennae. To which group does it belong?
parts.examinerComment: Arachnids have four pairs of legs and no antennae, a frequent distractor.

parts.prompt: Which structure is found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A cell is 0.05 mm long. In a drawing it is 40 mm long. What is the magnification of the drawing?
parts.examinerComment: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size, with both in the same units.

parts.prompt: Pieces of potato are placed in a concentrated sugar solution for one hour. What happens to the potato pieces?

options.text: They gain mass because water enters by osmosis.
They gain mass because sugar enters by diffusion.
They lose mass because water leaves by osmosis.
They lose mass because sugar leaves by active transport.

markingPoints.text: C – water moves from higher water potential (in the cells) to lower water potential (the solution)

parts.examinerComment: Answers should refer to water potential, not 'sugar concentration', when explaining osmosis.

parts.prompt: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from soil where the ion concentration is lower than inside the cell. Which process is used?

markingPoints.text: A – active transport moves ions against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A food sample turns biuret solution from blue to purple. Which nutrient is present?
parts.examinerComment: Candidates should learn each food test with its positive result.

parts.prompt: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction decrease above the optimum temperature?

options.text: The enzyme molecules have less kinetic energy.
The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.
The substrate is used up more quickly.

markingPoints.text: B – denaturation changes the shape of the active site

parts.examinerComment: Enzymes are proteins, not living organisms, so they are denatured, not 'killed'.

questions.stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on the activity of amylase.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the substrate and the product of amylase.
parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave 'glucose' as the product, which was not accepted.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the activity of amylase increases as the temperature increases from 20 °C to 35 °C.

markingPoints.text: molecules gain kinetic energy / move faster
more (successful) collisions between enzyme and substrate
more enzyme–substrate complexes formed (per unit time)

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers used the terms kinetic energy, collisions and enzyme–substrate complex. Vague references to enzymes 'working harder' gained no credit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define the term osmosis.

markingPoints.text: from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential

parts.examinerComment: Definitions must refer to water molecules and a partially permeable membrane. 'Semi-permeable' was accepted.

parts.prompt: Which substance enters a leaf through the stomata and is used in photosynthesis?
parts.examinerComment: Oxygen was a common wrong answer. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis and leaves through the stomata.

parts.prompt: Why do plants need magnesium ions?
parts.examinerComment: Candidates often confused magnesium with nitrate ions, which are needed to make amino acids.

parts.prompt: Where in the body is bile made?
parts.examinerComment: Many chose the gall bladder. Bile is made in the liver and only stored in the gall bladder.

parts.prompt: Which enzyme digests protein in the stomach?
parts.examinerComment: Trypsin also digests protein, but it works in the small intestine, not the stomach.

parts.prompt: Which tissue transports sucrose from the leaves to other parts of a plant?
parts.examinerComment: Xylem transports water and mineral ions; phloem transports sucrose and amino acids.

parts.prompt: Which condition increases the rate of transpiration?
parts.examinerComment: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the concentration gradient steep.

parts.prompt: Which blood vessel carries blood from the lungs to the heart?
parts.examinerComment: Remember that veins carry blood towards the heart, even when that blood is oxygenated.

parts.prompt: Which component of blood transports oxygen?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: What is a pathogen?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered. Option C describes an antibody.

parts.prompt: How does a vaccine protect a person against a disease?

options.text: It contains antibiotics that kill the pathogen.
It contains antibodies that destroy the pathogen.
It contains antigens that stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells.
It contains white blood cells that engulf the pathogen.

markingPoints.text: C – It contains antigens that stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells.

parts.examinerComment: Option B describes passive immunity. A vaccine gives active immunity because the body makes its own antibodies.

parts.prompt: Which feature of the alveoli increases the rate of gas exchange?
parts.examinerComment: A thin wall gives a short diffusion distance. Candidates should be able to list all the features of a gas exchange surface.

parts.prompt: What happens to the ribcage when the external intercostal muscles contract?

markingPoints.text: B – It moves up and out.

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: What is produced by anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?
parts.examinerComment: Ethanol and carbon dioxide are produced by anaerobic respiration in yeast, not in muscles.

parts.prompt: In which part of a cell does most aerobic respiration take place?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Which organ breaks down excess amino acids to form urea?
parts.examinerComment: Many chose the kidney. The kidney removes urea from the blood, but urea is made in the liver.

parts.prompt: Which substance is normally absent from the urine of a healthy person?
parts.examinerComment: Glucose is filtered out of the blood in the kidney, but all of it is normally reabsorbed.

parts.prompt: Which hormone lowers the concentration of glucose in the blood?
parts.examinerComment: Glucagon raises blood glucose. Learning the two hormones as a pair helps avoid confusion.

parts.prompt: Which part of the eye contains the light-sensitive receptor cells?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes a drug?

options.text: any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
any substance made by a doctor

markingPoints.text: B – any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body

parts.examinerComment: The syllabus definition is broad and includes medicines and recreational substances.

parts.prompt: Why should patients finish a full course of antibiotics?

options.text: to make the antibiotic work faster
to reduce the chance of resistant bacteria surviving and spreading
to stop the body making antibodies

markingPoints.text: C – to reduce the chance of resistant bacteria surviving and spreading

parts.examinerComment: Option B was a common error. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

parts.prompt: Where does fertilisation usually take place in humans?
parts.examinerComment: Many chose the uterus. The embryo implants in the uterus after fertilisation in the oviduct.

parts.prompt: Which is a feature of insect-pollinated flowers?
parts.examinerComment: The other three options are features of wind-pollinated flowers.

parts.prompt: What is an allele?

options.text: a length of DNA that codes for a protein
a change in a base sequence

markingPoints.text: B – a version of a gene

parts.examinerComment: Option A describes a gene. Candidates should use the terms gene and allele precisely.

parts.prompt: Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt) are crossed. T (tall) is dominant to t (short). What is the expected ratio of tall to short offspring?
parts.examinerComment: A Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt: three tall to one short.

parts.prompt: Which is an example of continuous variation in humans?
parts.examinerComment: Continuous variation has a range of values with no distinct categories.

parts.prompt: What is the original source of new alleles in a population?
parts.examinerComment: Sexual reproduction creates new combinations of alleles, but only mutation creates new alleles.

parts.prompt: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, which organism is the secondary consumer?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Why is the transfer of energy between trophic levels inefficient?

options.text: Energy is destroyed at each level.
Energy is lost to the environment, for example as heat from respiration.
Producers do not absorb any light energy.

markingPoints.text: B – Energy is lost to the environment, for example as heat from respiration.

parts.examinerComment: Option A was a common error. Energy is not destroyed; it is transferred to the environment.

parts.prompt: Which gas released by burning fossil fuels contributes most to the enhanced greenhouse effect?
parts.examinerComment: Sulfur dioxide was a common distractor. It causes acid rain, not the enhanced greenhouse effect.

parts.prompt: Fertiliser runs off farmland into a lake. What happens first?
parts.examinerComment: Candidates should learn the sequence of eutrophication in order: algal growth, light blocked, plants die, decomposers respire, oxygen falls, fish die.

parts.prompt: Why are bacteria useful in biotechnology?
parts.examinerComment: Other good reasons are that they have plasmids and there are few ethical concerns over their use.

parts.prompt: Which enzyme is used to cut DNA at specific sites in genetic modification?
parts.examinerComment: DNA ligase joins pieces of DNA; restriction enzymes cut them.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.

markingPoints.text: correct formulae: CO₂ and H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ and O₂

parts.examinerComment: Light and chlorophyll may be written above the arrow. The most common error was balancing oxygen incorrectly.

parts.prompt: Explain how bile helps in the digestion of fats.

markingPoints.text: increases the surface area for lipase to act on
bile neutralises stomach acid, giving the optimum pH for enzymes in the small intestine

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates wrote that bile digests fats. Bile is not an enzyme: it emulsifies fats so that lipase works faster.

parts.prompt: Define transpiration.

markingPoints.text: loss of water vapour from leaves
by evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion of water vapour through the stomata

parts.examinerComment: Definitions that said only 'loss of water' did not gain full credit. The answer must refer to water vapour.

parts.prompt: A person's heart beats 72 times per minute. It pumps 70 cm³ of blood with each beat. Calculate the volume of blood pumped in one minute, in cm³.
parts.examinerComment: Most candidates multiplied correctly. A few divided, giving an answer smaller than one beat's volume.

parts.prompt: Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat diseases caused by viruses.

markingPoints.text: antibiotics act on structures or processes found in bacteria, e.g. the cell wall
viruses do not have these structures / are not cells

parts.examinerComment: Answers saying viruses are 'too strong' or 'immune' gained no credit.

parts.prompt: State two differences between the composition of inspired air and expired air.

markingPoints.text: expired air contains more carbon dioxide
expired air contains more water vapour

parts.examinerComment: Answers must be comparative: 'expired air has carbon dioxide' was not enough, since inspired air contains some too.

parts.prompt: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
parts.examinerComment: Some candidates added 'energy' as a product. This was ignored, but energy is not a substance.

parts.prompt: Explain why glucose is not normally found in the urine of a healthy person.

markingPoints.text: glucose is filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus
all of it is reabsorbed (into the blood) in the tubule of the nephron

parts.examinerComment: Many said glucose is 'not filtered'. It is filtered, then reabsorbed.

parts.prompt: Describe the pathway of a nerve impulse in a reflex arc, from receptor to effector.

markingPoints.text: impulse travels from the receptor along a sensory neurone
to a relay neurone in the spinal cord / CNS
then along a motor neurone to the effector (muscle or gland)

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers named all three types of neurone in the correct order.

parts.prompt: Explain how overuse of antibiotics can lead to populations of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

markingPoints.text: a random mutation makes some bacteria resistant
the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria
passing on the resistance allele / gene

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should avoid saying bacteria 'become used to' or 'learn to resist' antibiotics.

parts.prompt: State two advantages of asexual reproduction for a plant.

markingPoints.text: offspring are identical, so are well suited to the same environment

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A plant with genotype Tt is crossed with a plant with genotype tt. T (tall) is dominant to t (short). What percentage of the offspring are expected to be short?
parts.examinerComment: Candidates who drew a Punnett square were more successful.

parts.prompt: Explain the difference between natural selection and artificial selection.

markingPoints.text: in natural selection, the environment / selection pressures decide which individuals survive and reproduce
in artificial selection, humans choose individuals with desired features to breed

parts.examinerComment: Both processes needed to be described for full marks.

parts.prompt: A producer contains 10 000 kJ of energy. 10% of this energy passes to the primary consumer. How much energy does the primary consumer receive, in kJ?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Describe how deforestation can increase the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

markingPoints.text: fewer trees photosynthesise, so less carbon dioxide is absorbed
decomposers break down dead wood and release carbon dioxide by respiration

parts.examinerComment: Many described only one process. Questions worth three marks usually need three distinct points.

parts.prompt: Explain why pectinase is used in the production of fruit juice.

markingPoints.text: pectinase breaks down pectin in plant cell walls
so more juice is extracted / the juice is clearer

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

questions.stem: Fig. 1 shows the effect of temperature on the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction.

figures.alt: Graph of rate of reaction against temperature for an enzyme: the rate rises from 5 at 0 °C to a peak of 90 at 40 °C, then falls to 0 at 60 °C.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the optimum temperature for this enzyme, in °C.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the rate of reaction is zero at 60 °C.

markingPoints.text: the shape of the active site has changed
the substrate no longer fits / no enzyme–substrate complexes form

parts.examinerComment: Enzymes are not 'killed'.

questions.stem: Fig. 2 shows how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis at two concentrations of carbon dioxide.

figures.alt: Graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two carbon dioxide concentrations. Both lines rise together. At 0.04% carbon dioxide the rate levels off at 30 from light intensity 3; at 0.10% it levels off at 50 from light intensity 5.
figures.caption: Fig. 2

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the maximum rate of photosynthesis at 0.04% carbon dioxide, in arbitrary units.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis at 0.04% carbon dioxide above a light intensity of 4 units. Explain how Fig. 2 shows this.

markingPoints.text: increasing light intensity has no effect, but increasing carbon dioxide raises the rate

parts.examinerComment: Use evidence from both lines on the graph.
